name: Science-based lifting (SBL)

lead: Science-based lifting (SBL) is a way of organising resistance training around what hypertrophy research has found about muscle growth. Its payoff for appearance is direct: more muscle on the shoulders, chest, back and arms changes the silhouette, and the approach is popular with people who want that result in fewer, harder sets.

The approach emphasises weekly volume, sets taken close to failure, progressive overload and training each muscle about twice a week. Research on these variables comes from controlled training studies and reviews, while SBL as a packaged style is mostly spread through YouTube, TikTok and forum guides.

paras: Practitioners pick exercises that load a muscle through a long range of motion and that they find comfortable, train each muscle group roughly twice weekly, take working sets near failure, and add load or reps over time. Some versions use fewer sets than traditional bodybuilding splits. Results depend on consistency, food intake and sleep over months to years.

Training near failure raises soreness and fatigue, and heavy lifting carries the usual strain and joint injury risks if form or recovery is poor. Guides written by hobbyists may contain errors; one forum guide's own author notes having no formal qualification and invites corrections.

angle.text: SBL aims to make each hard set count toward muscle growth so lifters gain size efficiently. People use it to build a V-taper and fuller limbs, with the exact program left to personal preference and recovery.

lead: Science-based lifting (SBL) is a label used in fitness and looksmaxxing communities for resistance training built around findings from hypertrophy (muscle growth) research. Followers use it to add muscle size, which changes shoulder width, arm and chest fullness and overall body proportion.[1][2]

Common themes are enough weekly volume, hard sets stopped within a couple of repetitions of failure, progressive overload, and training each muscle about twice a week.[2] Writers in the style often favour fewer, more intense sets rather than very long sessions. A looksmax.org guide presents SBL as a set of principles rather than a fixed program, and stresses that an exercise the lifter enjoys and tolerates can outperform a theoretically ideal one they dislike.[1]

Strength-training research supports a positive relationship between volume and growth and a benefit from training a muscle twice weekly versus once, while questions such as whether a third session adds more remain open.[2]
infobox: Volume, proximity to failure, progressive overload[2]

paras: SBL is not a single program. It is a shared vocabulary of training variables - volume, intensity, effort, frequency, exercise selection and progression - that followers adjust to their own schedule and recovery.[1][2]

A looksmax.org guide titled as a full guide to SBL describes itself as a summary of principles learned from TikTok, YouTube and PubMed reading, not a list of workouts, and says personal enjoyment of an exercise affects results.[1] A reply in the thread corrected a point about sarcoplasmic versus stretch-mediated hypertrophy, and the author said they would look into it.[1]

The strength-training literature reports a positive relationship between the number of sets, repetitions and load and the amount of muscle gained, and volume is described as one of the most important training variables.[2]

Muscle growth has been reported across a wide range of loads, with 60-80% of one-rep max for 8-12 repetitions often given as a typical range. Sets taken to within roughly two or three repetitions of failure are described as sufficient for growth without necessarily reaching complete failure.[2]

Training a muscle twice per week has been reported to produce more growth than once weekly; whether three times is better is unresolved. Repetition speeds from about half a second to eight seconds give similar growth, and very slow reps beyond roughly ten seconds do less.[2]

No studies found on SBL as a named approach. The underlying variables (volume, frequency, effort) have been examined in resistance-training research, summarised in general strength-training references.[2]

On looksmax.org the label appears in guides aimed at 'gymcels' who want to improve their physique, with authors contrasting it with advice they consider poorly grounded.[1] Participants correct one another on mechanisms and exercise choice, so the content ranges from well-sourced to anecdotal.

lore.intro: Forum users share SBL as a corrective to bro-split training advice, usually in the form of principle lists and personal experience.[1]
